explanation: Comments say what something is; tags say what class of thing it is, and only the second is queryable at scale. "Show me everything holding PII" is a query over column_tags, not a text search over free prose that different authors wrote differently.

why.B: Comments are in information_schema.columns; they are just not structured.
why.C: A LIKE over prose misses every column whose author wrote "personal", "sensitive" or nothing.
why.D: Column tags exist and have their own information_schema view.

stem: An analyst builds a table inventory from information_schema.tables and reports 120 tables. An admin runs the identical query and gets 340. Neither query has a WHERE clause. What explains the difference?

options.A: information_schema is filtered by the caller's privileges; each user sees only the objects they can access, so an inventory is only complete when run by a principal that can see everything.
options.B: The analyst queried the per-catalog view and the admin queried system.information_schema, which spans all catalogs.
options.C: The admin's query included temporary views.
options.D: Caching; the analyst's result was stale.

explanation: The views are filtered by what the caller may see. That is a feature, and a trap for anyone building governance reports: the same inventory built by two people is two different inventories.

why.B: The question says the queries were identical; the difference is the caller.
why.C: Temporary views are not in information_schema.tables.
why.D: information_schema is not a cached snapshot per user.

stem: An access review finds group finance has SELECT on hr.salaries. An engineer runs REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE hr.salaries FROM finance, which succeeds, but the group can still read the table. Why?

options.A: The privilege was granted on the schema (or catalog) and inherited; revoking on the table removes a grant that was never there. Revoke it where it lives, as SHOW GRANTS' ObjectType or table_privileges.inherited_from shows.
options.B: Revokes take effect at the next cluster restart.
options.C: finance is also the owner of the table, and owners cannot be revoked.
options.D: The group holds SELECT through a row filter that must be dropped first.

explanation: A privilege applies where it inherits but lives where it was granted. The revoke reported success and changed nothing, which is why an access review must record the level a grant was made at, not only that it applies.

why.B: Grants and revokes apply immediately.
why.C: Ownership is possible but not implied; the common cause is inheritance.
why.D: Row filters restrict rows; they do not grant privileges.

stem: A service principal is granted SELECT on every table in catalog reporting via a catalog-level grant, yet its queries fail with PERMISSION_DENIED on every table. information_schema.table_privileges shows the SELECT. What is missing?

options.A: USE CATALOG on the catalog and USE SCHEMA on each schema; SELECT is inert without the traversal privileges, and no privileges view computes that conjunction for you.
options.B: Table ownership; only owners can exercise inherited grants.
options.C: A refresh of the catalog's privilege cache.
options.D: A workspace binding; service principals cannot read catalogs at all.

explanation: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are the right to see that something exists and name it. Holding SELECT without them is the classic support ticket, and it is invisible to a report built from table_privileges alone.

why.B: Inherited grants work for any grantee; ownership is not required.
why.C: There is no privilege cache to refresh.
why.D: Service principals are ordinary principals in Unity Catalog.

stem: A dimension's surrogate key is generated with monotonically_increasing_id() each time the dimension is rebuilt. Facts published last month reference those keys. What goes wrong at the next rebuild, and what fixes it?

options.A: Keys are renumbered, so every published fact points at a different version; derive the key deterministically, for example a hash of the natural key and valid_from.
options.B: Nothing; monotonically_increasing_id() is stable across runs for the same input.
options.C: Keys collide within the rebuild, causing duplicate rows.
options.D: The rebuild fails because surrogate keys must be sequential integers.

explanation: A scalable model must survive a rebuild. Generated ids depend on partition layout and run order; a hash of the identifying columns produces the same key for the same version every time, so facts already published keep pointing at the right row.

why.B: The function is deterministic only within a run's layout; another run assigns different ids.
why.C: Ids within one run are unique; instability across runs is the problem.
why.D: Surrogate keys can be any unique value; strings from a hash are common.

stem: An order fact is joined to a Type 2 customer dimension on customer_id only. 900 orders go in and 1,180 rows come out, with no error. What happened, and what is the correct join?

options.A: Customers with several versions matched every version; join on customer_id AND ordered_on >= valid_from AND ordered_on < valid_to so each order matches the one version in effect on its date.
options.B: The dimension has duplicate natural keys by mistake; deduplicate it first.
options.C: The fact table has duplicate orders; deduplicate the fact.
options.D: The join should be a LEFT ANTI join to remove unmatched orders.

explanation: A dimension join must not change the fact's row count. In a Type 2 dimension the natural key identifies a customer, not a row, so the validity window belongs in the join condition, with asymmetric bounds so a changeover date matches exactly one version.

why.B: Several versions per key is the definition of a Type 2 dimension, not a mistake.
why.C: The fact had 900 distinct orders; the growth came from the join.
why.D: An anti join removes matches; the fix is to match exactly one version.

stem: A new fact table's query patterns are not yet known. The team must choose a layout today. Which choice keeps the most options open at the least cost?

options.A: CLUSTER BY AUTO, letting Databricks choose and revise keys from query history; keys can be changed later without rewriting the table.
options.B: PARTITIONED BY the date column, since it is always safe.
options.C: ZORDER BY every column that might be filtered, run after each load.
options.D: No layout at all until the patterns are known, then partition.

explanation: Clustering is a property of the table the engine maintains and that you can change; partitioning is a directory layout fixed at creation. Not knowing the access pattern is the normal state at creation time, and AUTO is built for it.

why.B: A daily partition on a table that is not large per day produces small files, and the choice cannot be undone without a rewrite.
why.C: ZORDER is not incremental and re-sorts everything each run; more columns dilute it.
why.D: Partitioning later still means rewriting the table; clustering later is a metadata change.

stem: A table partitioned by region has one partition ten times larger than the others and thousands of tiny files in the smallest ones. Queries filtering on region are slow for the big region and slow to list for the small ones. Which benefit of liquid clustering addresses both symptoms?

options.A: Clustering targets file size rather than one directory per value, so a hot key is spread across files and small keys are grouped into full files.
options.B: Clustering creates a directory per region like partitioning but compresses them.
options.C: Clustering removes the need for statistics, so file counts stop mattering.
options.D: Clustering only helps the small partitions; the large region needs ZORDER.

explanation: A partition is exactly as big as its key value says, so skew becomes a straggler directory and sparse keys become tiny files. Clustering groups rows into files by the key with no directories, targeting file size, and its OPTIMIZE is incremental.

why.B: Clustering has no directories; that is the difference.
why.C: Statistics are what make skipping possible; clustering provides the locality for them.
why.D: ZORDER re-sorts everything each run and does not fix the partition layout.

stem: A team reloads one calendar month of a very large table every night by deleting and rewriting that month. Partitions are several gigabytes each. Which layout is the better fit, and why?

options.A: Partitioning by month: REPLACE WHERE on the partition column drops the old slice's files by metadata alone and writes only the new month, and the partitions are large enough to be worth it.
options.B: Liquid clustering by month, because clustering is always preferred.
options.C: No layout; deletes and rewrites are cheap regardless.
options.D: ZORDER by month, run after each nightly load.

explanation: "Always cluster" is not the lesson. Partitioning still wins when partitions are comfortably large and whole slices are dropped or overwritten, because REPLACE WHERE on a partition column has no clustering equivalent.

why.B: Clustering cannot swap a slice cheaply; the overwrite becomes a row-level rewrite.
why.C: A month of a very large table is not cheap to delete and rewrite row by row.
why.D: ZORDER is a sort within files and does nothing for slice replacement.

stem: A job fails with a long stack trace whose first line reads "[CAST_INVALID_INPUT] The value '12 units' of the type STRING cannot be cast to INT". What is the most reliable thing to search for and act on?

options.A: The error class CAST_INVALID_INPUT, which is stable across releases and documented; then find the rows with try_cast to see what would not convert.
options.B: The full stack trace, pasted into a search engine.
options.C: The line number in the notebook, which identifies the failing cell.
options.D: The cluster's driver log, which has the real cause.

explanation: Databricks error messages carry a stable error class and SQLSTATE; the prose changes between versions, the class does not. try_cast then turns "it failed" into a list of the responsible rows.

why.B: Stack traces are noisy and version-specific; the class is the searchable key.
why.C: The cell tells you where, not why; the message already names the value.
why.D: The message on the run already names the cause; logs are for when it does not, and are unavailable on serverless.

stem: A nightly job that usually takes 15 minutes took 70 last night and succeeded. An engineer opens the cluster logs first. What is the better first step, and why?

options.A: Compare the run's task durations with previous runs in the run history to localise which task slowed, then open that task's Spark UI; logs come last.
options.B: Opening the logs is right; they contain the most detail.
options.C: Re-run the job to see whether it is slow again before investigating.
options.D: Check system.billing.usage to see whether the run cost more.

explanation: Start narrow. Run history shows which task changed; the Spark UI for that task shows the stage and whether it skewed or spilled. Reading logs before knowing where to look wastes the easy answer.

why.B: Detail without a target is noise; and serverless runs have no cluster logs at all.
why.C: Re-running discards the evidence you already have and costs another 70 minutes.
why.D: Cost confirms it was slow; it does not say where.

stem: A four-task job failed at task 3. Tasks 1 and 2 each appended rows to Delta tables and succeeded. The engineer repairs the run. What happens?

options.A: Only task 3 and its dependants re-run; tasks 1 and 2 are not repeated and their commits stand.
options.B: All four tasks re-run from the start, so tasks 1 and 2 append their rows a second time.
options.C: Tasks 1 and 2 are rolled back and the whole job runs again.
options.D: The repair fails because appends cannot be part of a repairable job.

explanation: Repair re-executes failed tasks and the tasks that depend on them. Earlier successful commits are not rolled back and not repeated. The task being repaired does run again from its start, which is why tasks should be idempotent.

why.B: Successful tasks are skipped by repair; that is the difference from a fresh run.
why.C: Delta commits are durable; a job has no transaction spanning tasks.
why.D: Any job can be repaired; the append concern is about the repaired task, not the earlier ones.

stem: A job's task reads a cutoff date from a job parameter and failed because the upstream data for that date was late. The data has now arrived. What is the lightest correct way to complete the run?

options.A: Repair the run (or run-now), overriding the parameter if the date must change; no edit to the job definition is needed.
options.B: Edit the job's default parameter in the UI, redeploy, and start a new run.
options.C: Edit the notebook to hard-code the date, then repair the run.
options.D: Delete the failed run and create a new job for the late date.

explanation: Parameter overrides on repair and run-now exist for exactly this: re-run against a corrected input without touching the job definition. The definition stays the reviewed one; the override lives with the run.

why.B: Changing the default affects every future run and requires a deploy for a one-off.
why.C: Hard-coding in the notebook breaks the parameterisation permanently.
why.D: A new job duplicates configuration and loses the run's history.

stem: A declarative pipeline update failed. Which query surface shows the failing flow, its error class, and the expectation counts recorded before the failure, in one place?

options.A: The pipeline's event log, queried for that update id.
options.B: The pipeline's target table's DESCRIBE HISTORY.
options.C: The Jobs run list for the job that triggered the pipeline.
options.D: The SQL warehouse query history.

explanation: The event log records each update's flows, expectation results and errors. It is the pipeline equivalent of run history plus error message, and it is queryable as a table so the failure can be seen in context.

why.B: Table history records successful writes; a failed update leaves no commit to describe.
why.C: The job only knows the pipeline task failed; the flows are inside the pipeline.
why.D: Query history is for warehouse queries, not pipeline updates.

stem: A Structured Streaming job restarted after a deploy and reprocessed every file in its source, doubling the rows in the target. Nothing in the code changed. What most likely happened?

options.A: The checkpoint location changed or was deleted, so the stream had no memory of consumed files and started from the beginning.
options.B: The source folder was re-uploaded, which Auto Loader treats as new data.
options.C: The target table's transaction log was compacted, which resets the stream.
options.D: The trigger switched to availableNow, which reads everything each time.

explanation: The checkpoint is the stream's memory of what it has consumed. A new or deleted checkpoint path makes the stream start from scratch, and an append sink faithfully appends everything again with no error.

why.B: Identical re-uploaded files are not new to Auto Loader; its checkpoint records them.
why.C: Compaction of the target's log does not affect the source stream's progress.
why.D: availableNow processes what is new since the checkpoint, not everything.

stem: A CI pipeline runs databricks bundle validate -t prod and reports success. A teammate concludes the job's notebook has been tested. What is true?

options.A: validate checks configuration and resolves variables only; it runs no code. Tests need a separate step, and bundle run executes the job.
options.B: validate executes each job once in a dry-run mode, so the notebook did run.
options.C: validate deploys to a temporary target and runs the job there.
options.D: validate is equivalent to deploy without the upload step.

explanation: bundle validate is a configuration check. deploy uploads files and creates or updates resources; run triggers a job or deploys and starts an app. Testing is whatever the team adds to CI, and a green validate says nothing about it.

why.B: There is no dry-run execution of jobs in validate.
why.C: validate touches no target beyond resolving its configuration.
why.D: deploy creates and updates resources; validate creates nothing.

stem: A bundle deployed by CI as a service principal places its files under /Workspace/Users/<application-id>/.bundle/<name>/<target>/files. An engineer deploys the same bundle from a laptop with the same target and finds a second copy under their own home folder, and two jobs with different name prefixes. What does this demonstrate?

options.A: A deployment is namespaced by the deploying identity in development mode; one deployer per environment is the rule for production.
options.B: A bug: the second deploy should have overwritten the first.
options.C: The service principal lacks permission to write to the engineer's folder.
options.D: The target was misconfigured to production mode on one of the two machines.

explanation: The workspace path records who deployed, and development mode prefixes resources by deployer. Two deployers, two deployments. Production deployments use a single principal (usually CI) precisely to avoid this.

why.B: Not a bug; isolation per deployer is what development mode is for.
why.C: Each deployer writes to its own home; nobody wrote to anyone else's.
why.D: Both used development mode; that is why both have prefixes.

stem: A team edits notebooks in a Databricks Git folder linked to a feature branch, commits, and opens a pull request. Which statement about the workflow is accurate?

options.A: The Git folder tracks one branch at a time; switching branches changes every notebook in the folder, and the pull request's checks run in CI outside the workspace.
options.B: Each notebook in the Git folder can be on its own branch.
options.C: Committing from the Git folder deploys the notebooks to production automatically.
options.D: Git folders only support the main branch; feature branches must be handled locally.

explanation: A Git folder is a checkout of one branch in the workspace: edit and run there, commit, push, review in the Git provider. Deployment is a separate step, driven by CI on merge, not by the commit itself.

why.B: The folder is a single checkout; the branch applies to all of it.
why.C: A commit is a commit; deployment happens when a pipeline runs bundle deploy on merge.
why.D: Git folders check out any branch and can create them.

stem: An engineer tests the CI deploy locally by exporting DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID and DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET for the service principal and running bundle deploy. It succeeds, but the resources appear under the engineer's own user path. Why?

options.A: DATABRICKS_CONFIG_PROFILE was set in the shell, so the CLI resolved that profile and ignored the client credentials, deploying as the engineer.
options.B: Service principals always deploy under the invoking user's path.
options.C: The client secret had expired, and the CLI fell back to the user's browser session.
options.D: bundle deploy ignores environment variables; only the profile file counts.

explanation: A named profile takes precedence over machine-to-machine environment variables. The deploy quietly ran as the person, which is why a local test of CI authentication must unset the profile (env -u DATABRICKS_CONFIG_PROFILE) to mean anything.

why.B: A service-principal deploy lands under the principal's own path.
why.C: An expired secret fails authentication; it does not silently switch identity.
why.D: Environment variables are a supported auth method; the profile simply outranked them.

stem: A Delta Lake table was created with the first query below. Realizing that the original query had a typographical error, the second query was executed. Which result will occur after running the second command?
code:
CREATE TABLE prod.sales_by_stor
USING DELTA
LOCATION "/mnt/prod/sales_by_store"

ALTER TABLE prod.sales_by_stor RENAME TO prod.sales_by_store

options.A: All related files and metadata are dropped and recreated in a single ACID transaction.
options.B: The table name change is recorded in the Delta transaction log.
options.C: A new Delta transaction log is created for the renamed table.
options.D: The table reference in the metastore is updated.

explanation: The table was created with an explicit LOCATION, making it an external table. Renaming it changes only the metastore's pointer - no data files move, and the Delta transaction log is untouched. The key idea is the separation between the catalog (which names things) and the transaction log (which records data operations); a rename is purely a catalog operation.

why.A: Nothing is dropped or rewritten. A rename that moved terabytes of files would be a very expensive typo fix.
why.B: The transaction log records data operations on the table, not the name the catalog knows it by.
why.C: The log lives with the data at its storage location, which has not changed, so no new log is created.

stem: A Structured Streaming job deployed to production has been experiencing delays during peak hours of the day. Currently, during normal execution, each microbatch of data is processed in under 3 seconds. During peak hours, execution time for each microbatch becomes very inconsistent, sometimes exceeding 30 seconds. The streaming write is currently configured with a 10-second trigger interval. Holding all other variables constant and assuming records need to be processed in less than 10 seconds, which adjustment will meet the requirement?

options.A: Use the trigger once option and configure a Databricks job to execute the query every 8 seconds; this ensures all backlogged records are processed with each batch.
options.B: Decrease the trigger interval to 5 seconds; triggering batches more frequently may prevent records from backing up and large batches from causing a spill.
options.C: Decrease the trigger interval to 5 seconds; triggering batches more frequently allows idle executors to begin processing the next batch while longer-running tasks from previous batches finish.
options.D: The trigger interval cannot be modified without modifying the checkpoint directory; to maintain the current stream state, increase the number of shuffle partitions to maximize parallelism.

explanation: Smaller, more frequent batches keep each microbatch's working set small enough to avoid spilling to disk, which is what makes peak-hour runtimes blow out to 30 seconds. Note that B and C recommend the same action - the exam is testing the *reasoning*, not the change. Read the justification, not just the verb.

why.A: Trigger-once processes all available data in one batch, which makes the batch larger, not smaller - the opposite of what is needed.
why.C: Right action, wrong mechanism. Structured Streaming microbatches run sequentially; the next batch does not start while the previous one is still finishing, so there are no idle executors overlapping work.
why.D: The trigger interval can be changed without touching the checkpoint. Trigger interval is not part of the checkpointed state.

stem: A Delta Lake table representing metadata about content posts from users has the schema below. Based on that schema, which column should be used for partitioning the Delta table?
code:
user_id     LONG,
post_text   STRING,
post_id     STRING,
longitude   FLOAT,
latitude    FLOAT,
post_time   TIMESTAMP,
date        DATE

options.A: post_id
options.B: post_time
options.C: date
options.D: user_id

explanation: A partition column needs low enough cardinality that each partition holds a substantial amount of data - the usual guidance is at least around a gigabyte per partition. `date` gives one partition per day, which is coarse enough to avoid a small-file explosion and aligns with how such data is usually queried. Worth knowing that modern Databricks guidance is to prefer Liquid Clustering over partitioning for most tables (see PRO-S10-O3); this question predates that shift and tests classic partition-column selection.

why.A: post_id is unique per row - one partition per post, which is the worst possible choice.
why.B: A TIMESTAMP has second or sub-second granularity, so partitioning on it creates an enormous number of tiny partitions.
why.D: user_id is high cardinality and skewed - a few prolific users would produce huge partitions while most produce trivial ones.

stem: A table named user_ltv is being used to create a view that will be used by data analysts on various teams. Users in the workspace are configured into groups, which are used for setting up data access using ACLs. The user_ltv table has the schema `email STRING, age INT, ltv INT`. The view definition below is executed, then an analyst who is NOT a member of the marketing group runs `SELECT * FROM email_ltv`. What will be the result of this query?
code:
CREATE VIEW email_ltv AS
SELECT
  CASE WHEN is_member('marketing') THEN email ELSE 'REDACTED' END AS email,
  ltv
FROM user_ltv

options.A: Only the email and ltv columns will be returned; the email column will contain the string "REDACTED" in each row.
options.B: Three columns will be returned, but one column will be named "REDACTED" and contain only null values.
options.C: Only the email and ltv columns will be returned; the email column will contain all null values.
options.D: The email and ltv columns will be returned with the values in user_ltv.

explanation: This is a dynamic view. `is_member('marketing')` is evaluated per querying user, so for a non-member the CASE yields the literal string 'REDACTED' in the email column. The view selects only email and ltv, so `age` never appears regardless of who asks - the view is the security boundary.

why.B: The column is aliased AS email; 'REDACTED' is the value, not the column name. And only two columns are selected.
why.C: The CASE returns a string literal, not NULL.
why.D: This is what a marketing group member would see. The whole point of is_member() is that the result differs by caller.

stem: The business reporting team requires that data for their dashboards be updated every hour. The total processing time for the pipeline, which extracts, transforms, and loads data for its runs, is 10 minutes. Assuming normal operating conditions, which configuration will meet their service-level agreement requirements with the lowest cost?

options.A: Schedule a job to execute the pipeline once an hour on a dedicated interactive cluster.
options.B: Schedule a job to execute the pipeline once an hour on a new job cluster.
options.C: Schedule a Structured Streaming job with a trigger interval of 60 minutes.
options.D: Configure a job that executes every time new data lands in a given directory.

explanation: A job cluster is created for the run and terminated when it finishes, so you pay for roughly 10 minutes of compute per hour instead of 60. Job clusters are also billed at a lower DBU rate than all-purpose compute. When a question pairs a fixed schedule with "lowest cost", job clusters are almost always the answer.

why.A: A dedicated interactive cluster runs continuously (or must be manually managed), so you pay for 60 minutes an hour to do 10 minutes of work - and at the higher all-purpose rate.
why.C: A streaming job keeps a cluster alive between triggers, which is the same always-on cost problem for what is fundamentally a batch workload.
why.D: File-arrival triggering does not meet a defined hourly SLA - it fires whenever data happens to land, which could be far more or less often than hourly.

stem: The security team is exploring whether the Databricks secrets module can be leveraged for connecting to an external database. After testing the code with all Python variables defined as plain strings, they upload the password to the secrets module and configure the correct permissions for the currently active user. They modify their code as below, leaving all other variables unchanged. What will happen when this code is executed?
code:
password = dbutils.secrets.get(scope="db_creds", key="jdbc_password")
print(password)

df = (spark.read
      .format("jdbc")
      .option("url", connection)
      .option("dbtable", tablename)
      .option("user", username)
      .option("password", password))

options.A: The connection to the external table will succeed; the string "REDACTED" will be printed.
options.B: The connection to the external table will succeed; the string value of the password will be printed in plain text.
options.C: An interactive input box will appear in the notebook; if the right password is provided, the connection will succeed, and the password will be printed in plain text.
options.D: An interactive input box will appear in the notebook; if the right password is provided, the connection will succeed, and the encoded password will be saved to DBFS.

explanation: Secrets retrieved via dbutils.secrets.get hold their real value in code - so the JDBC connection works - but Databricks redacts them from any notebook output. Printing one displays "REDACTED". This is a deliberate guardrail against accidentally leaking credentials into notebook results, logs or exported HTML.

why.B: This is precisely what redaction exists to prevent.
why.C: dbutils.secrets.get reads from the secret scope; it never prompts. You may be thinking of dbutils.widgets.
why.D: No prompt appears, and nothing is written to DBFS.

stem: A data ingestion task requires a 1-TB JSON dataset to be written out to Parquet with a target part-file size of 512 MB. Because Parquet is being used instead of Delta Lake, built-in file-sizing features such as Auto-Optimize and Auto-Compaction cannot be used. Which approach will work WITHOUT rearranging the data?

options.A: Ingest the data, execute the narrow transformations, repartition to 2,048 partitions, and then write to Parquet.
options.B: Set spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes to 512 MB, ingest the data, execute the narrow transformations, coalesce to 2,048 partitions, and then write to Parquet.
options.C: Set spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes to 512 MB, ingest the data, execute the narrow transformations, and then write to Parquet.
options.D: Set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 2,048 partitions, ingest the data, execute the narrow transformations, optimize the data by sorting it (which automatically repartitions the data), and then write to Parquet.

explanation: The constraint "without rearranging the data" is the whole question - it rules out any shuffle. `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` controls how much data each partition holds when files are *read*, so setting it to 512 MB gives partitions of roughly that size that flow through narrow transformations untouched and land as 512 MB output files. No shuffle occurs at any point.

why.A: repartition() is a full shuffle - exactly what the question forbids.
why.B: advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes applies to adaptive shuffle partitioning, and coalesce still rearranges data across partitions.
why.D: shuffle.partitions only affects operations that shuffle, and the sort explicitly repartitions.

stem: The marketing team wants to share data in an aggregate table with the sales organization, but the field names used by the teams do not match, and a number of marketing-specific fields have not been approved for the sales organization. Which solution addresses the situation while emphasizing simplicity?

options.A: Create a view on the marketing table selecting only those fields approved for the sales team; alias the names of any fields that should be standardized to the sales naming conventions.
options.B: Create a new table with the required schema and use Delta Lake's DEEP CLONE functionality to sync up changes committed to one table to the corresponding table.
options.C: Use a CTAS statement to create a derivative table from the marketing table, and then configure a production job to propagate the changes.
options.D: Add a parallel table write to the current production pipeline, updating a new sales table that varies as required from the marketing table.

explanation: A view solves both halves of the problem at once - column selection handles the unapproved fields, aliasing handles the naming mismatch - and it stays current automatically because it is computed at query time. Options B, C and D all create a second physical copy that must be kept in sync. When a question emphasizes "simplicity", prefer the solution that stores no duplicate data.

why.B: DEEP CLONE copies data and does not continuously sync; it also cannot rename or drop columns.
why.C: CTAS plus a propagation job is real duplication plus real operational burden, for something a view does for free.
why.D: A parallel write adds a second copy to maintain and a new failure mode in the production pipeline.

stem: A Databricks job has been configured with three tasks, each of which is a Databricks notebook. Task A does not depend on other tasks. Tasks B and C run in parallel, with each having a serial dependency on task A. What will be the resulting state if tasks A and B complete successfully but task C fails during a scheduled run?

options.A: All logic expressed in the notebook associated with tasks A and B will have been successfully completed; some operations in task C may have been completed successfully.
options.B: Unless all tasks are completed successfully, no changes will be committed to the Lakehouse; because task C failed, all commits will be rolled back automatically.
options.C: All logic expressed in the notebook associated with tasks A and B will have been successfully completed; any changes made in task C will be rolled back due to task failure.
options.D: Because all tasks are managed as a dependency graph, no changes will be committed to the Lakehouse until all tasks have successfully been completed.

explanation: Delta Lake gives ACID guarantees per *write operation*, not across a multi-task job. A job is not a distributed transaction: tasks A and B committed their writes and those stand, and task C may have committed several writes before failing partway through. This is why idempotent, restartable task design matters - the platform will not undo partial work for you.

why.B: There is no job-level transaction to roll back. Committed writes from A and B are durable.
why.C: Only the individual write that was in flight when C failed is rolled back; writes C already committed remain.
why.D: The dependency graph controls execution *order*, not transactional atomicity.

stem: Under AUTO CDC with SEQUENCE BY seq_num and APPLY AS DELETE WHEN op = 'delete', key K receives: update seq 5, delete seq 7, update seq 6. What is in the target?

options.A: No row for K; the delete at seq 7 is the highest sequence, so the later-arriving update at seq 6 is ignored.
options.B: A row for K from the seq 6 update, because it arrived last.
options.C: A row for K from the seq 5 update, because the delete removed only the later state.
options.D: An error, because a delete cannot be followed by an update.

explanation: Arrival order is irrelevant; sequence decides. The highest sequence for K is the delete, so K is absent. Had the update carried seq 8, K would be present again: deleted-then-resurrected keys are exactly what sequencing gets right.

why.B: Arrival order is what SEQUENCE BY exists to override.
why.C: Deletes remove the key; there is no partial state to fall back to.
why.D: Out-of-order and post-delete events are normal in a change feed.

stem: In one sentence: what property of the source decides between a streaming table and a materialized view?

options.A: Whether rows already loaded can change; if they can, a streaming table will not see the change.
options.B: Whether the source is large; large sources need streaming tables.
options.C: Whether the source is a file location or a table.
options.D: Whether the refresh is scheduled or continuous.

explanation: A streaming table consumes each row once; a materialized view recomputes. Append-only sources suit the first; sources whose old rows are updated or deleted need the second.

why.B: Size affects cost, not correctness; a large mutable source still needs the view.
why.C: Both objects can read tables and files.
why.D: Both can be scheduled or continuous.

stem: After unionByName of five sources, the revision column is BIGINT although the contract says INT, and no source declared BIGINT. What happened?

options.A: One source's inference produced a wider type and the union kept the widest; the types must be cast explicitly before or after the union.
options.B: unionByName always widens integer columns for safety.
options.C: Delta stores every integer as BIGINT.
options.D: The contract is wrong; INT cannot hold revision numbers.

explanation: A union takes the widest compatible type among its inputs. Inference is not declaration: one source inferring a long is enough to change the table's schema, which is why types are pinned rather than accepted.

why.B: The union widens only when an input is wider.
why.C: Delta stores the type it is given.
why.D: The contract is the specification; the pipeline must meet it.

stem: A bronze table has exactly twice the expected rows after a deploy, with no error in any run. Which change in the deploy is the most likely cause?

options.A: The stream's checkpoint path changed.
options.B: The trigger changed from availableNow to a processing-time interval.
options.C: The output mode changed from append to update.
options.D: The source folder was renamed.

explanation: A new checkpoint has no memory of consumed files, so the stream re-ingests everything and an append sink faithfully appends it again. Nothing raises; the count is the only evidence.

why.B: Trigger cadence changes when data is processed, not whether it is reprocessed.
why.C: Update mode on a file source would fail or change semantics loudly, not double rows.
why.D: A renamed source is an empty source, which loads nothing.

stem: A window frame must cover the previous 30 minutes of an irregular sensor series. Which frame is correct?

options.A: RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 30 MINUTES PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, ordered by the timestamp.
options.B: ROWS BETWEEN 30 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, ordered by the timestamp.
options.C: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, assuming 15-minute cadence.
options.D: RANGE BETWEEN 30 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW on the row number.

explanation: Time is a value of the ordering column, so the frame must be a range over it. Row counts assume a cadence the series does not keep; on an irregular series the difference is not subtle.

why.B: Thirty rows back is thirty readings, not thirty minutes.
why.C: The cadence assumption is exactly what irregular data violates.
why.D: A range over row numbers is a row frame in disguise.

stem: Match each expectation action to its effect: EXPECT alone; ON VIOLATION DROP ROW; ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE.

options.A: Count and keep the row; remove the row and continue; stop the update.
options.B: Remove the row; count and keep; stop the update.
options.C: Stop the update; remove the row; count and keep.
options.D: Count and keep; stop the update; remove the row.

explanation: A bare expectation records violations and lets the row through; DROP ROW removes it and continues; FAIL UPDATE halts the pipeline. Quarantine is the fourth option, built from DROP ROW plus a second table selecting the inverse.

why.B: Reversed for the first two.
why.C: Every action mismatched.
why.D: The last two are swapped.

stem: ALTER SHARE s ADD TABLE t WITHOUT HISTORY is refused. Which two statements, in order, make it succeed?

options.A: ALTER TABLE t SET TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableDeletionVectors = false); then REORG TABLE t APPLY (PURGE).
options.B: VACUUM t; then OPTIMIZE t.
options.C: ALTER TABLE t SET TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = false); then ALTER SHARE s REMOVE TABLE t.
options.D: DROP SHARE s; then CREATE SHARE s WITHOUT HISTORY.

explanation: Current-state sharing needs the data files alone to represent the table, which deletion vectors prevent. Turning the property off stops new vectors; the purge rewrites the files that still carry them.

why.B: Neither touches deletion vectors.
why.C: Change data feed is unrelated, and removing the table undoes the goal.
why.D: History is a per-object choice at ADD TABLE, not a share-level one.

stem: What is the only reliable proof that a newly configured foreign catalog works?

options.A: A query against a foreign table returning rows.
options.B: CREATE FOREIGN CATALOG succeeding.
options.C: The connection appearing in system.information_schema.connections.
options.D: bundle validate passing on the resource definitions.

explanation: Federation DDL is lazy; every step up to the first data access is metadata. Only touching the source exercises the credential and the network path.

why.B: Succeeds against a host that does not exist.
why.C: Lists the metadata that was accepted without validation.
why.D: Validates configuration, never connectivity.

stem: Weekend volume is a third of weekday volume. A degradation lowers weekday volume by 20%. Which comparison detects the degradation without firing on weekends?

options.A: Each day against a rolling baseline of the same day type, alerting on a sustained shortfall.
options.B: Each day against the previous day.
options.C: Each day against a fixed floor set just below the weekday minimum.
options.D: Each day against the 7-day overall average.

explanation: Like with like. A same-day-type baseline compares Saturday to recent Saturdays, so weekends are normal and a 20% weekday shortfall stands out. Any comparison that mixes day types either fires on weekends or hides the weekday drop.

why.B: Every Saturday looks like a collapse against Friday.
why.C: A floor below the weekday minimum is above the weekend maximum, so it fires every weekend.
why.D: The overall average sits between the two regimes; weekdays 20% down can still clear it.

stem: Which system table answers "how many DBUs did each job consume last week"?

options.A: system.billing.usage
options.B: system.access.audit
options.C: system.access.table_lineage
options.D: system.compute.clusters

explanation: Usage is the billing table: consumption per SKU with the workload identifiers and tags to group by. Audit is actions, lineage is data flow, clusters is compute configuration.

why.B: Records who did what, not what it cost.
why.C: Records which tables fed which.
why.D: Describes compute resources, not their consumption.

stem: Data skipping needs two things. A table has one of them and still reads every file for a selective filter. Which is missing, and what supplies it?

options.A: Locality; statistics exist, but values are scattered across files. Clustering on the filter column supplies it.
options.B: Statistics; clustering exists, but min/max were never collected. ANALYZE TABLE supplies them.
options.C: A partition; skipping only works on partition columns.
options.D: A ZORDER; statistics require a sort.

explanation: Delta collects min/max per file automatically; what it cannot do is make those ranges narrow. Locality comes from layout, and liquid clustering is how you give a column narrow per-file ranges without partitioning.

why.B: File statistics are collected on write, not by ANALYZE.
why.C: Skipping uses file statistics on any column with locality.
why.D: ZORDER is one way to get locality, and not the recommended one.

stem: A 40 MB dimension is shuffled in a join. Which single setting explains why the optimiser did not broadcast it, and what is its default?

options.A: spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, default 10 MB.
options.B: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, default 200.
options.C: spark.sql.adaptive.enabled, default true.
options.D: spark.databricks.io.cache.enabled, default false.

explanation: Tables under the threshold are broadcast automatically; 40 MB is above the default, so the planner chose a shuffle join. Raise the threshold or broadcast explicitly.

why.B: Controls shuffle parallelism, not the join strategy.
why.C: Adaptive execution can convert to broadcast at runtime, but the threshold still gates it.
why.D: The disk cache is unrelated to join planning.

stem: After DELETE, which two settings or commands make an erasure final, and what do they cost?

options.A: Shorten delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration and run VACUUM; time travel over that window is gone and concurrent readers may be disrupted.
options.B: OPTIMIZE and REORG; nothing, they are routine maintenance.
options.C: DROP TABLE and recreate it; the whole history is lost.
options.D: Disable change data feed and OPTIMIZE; the feed stops.

explanation: Deleted rows live on in earlier versions until the files are unreferenced and vacuumed. Retaining zero hours is right for an erasure request and wrong as a default; the cost is the loss of time travel for that window.

why.B: Neither removes files still referenced by retained history.
why.C: Destroys every row, not just the erased subject's.
why.D: CDF is unrelated to file retention.

stem: Which of these values needs a salt before hashing, and why?

options.A: A postcode; the input space is small enough to enumerate and match.
options.B: A UUID; hashes of random values are weak.
options.C: An email address; hashing strips the domain.
options.D: None; SHA-256 is irreversible for any input.

explanation: Irreversible is not the same as unguessable. A few thousand postcodes can all be hashed and compared; a salt kept out of the dataset makes that table useless. High-entropy values like UUIDs or emails do not need it.

why.B: Random 128-bit values cannot be enumerated.
why.C: Hashing does nothing to the domain; and email space is too large to enumerate.
why.D: Irreversibility does not protect a small input space.

stem: Which column tells an auditor where a SELECT on a table was actually granted, and what value means "on this table"?

options.A: information_schema.table_privileges.inherited_from; NONE.
options.B: information_schema.table_privileges.grantor; the table owner.
options.C: SHOW GRANTS' Principal column; the table name.
options.D: information_schema.tables.table_owner; NONE.

explanation: inherited_from records SCHEMA or CATALOG for an inherited privilege and NONE for one granted directly. The obvious three-column query omits it, and the result looks complete without it.

why.B: The grantor is who granted it, not at which level.
why.C: SHOW GRANTS carries the level in ObjectType, not Principal.
why.D: Ownership is a different fact, and the column has no NONE value.

stem: Complete the query that lists PII columns across a catalog: SELECT table_name, column_name FROM cat.information_schema.___ WHERE tag_name = 'pii'.

options.A: column_tags
options.B: columns
options.C: table_tags
options.D: column_masks

explanation: Column tags live in their own view. columns has comments and types, table_tags is table-level, and column_masks records mask functions rather than classifications.

why.B: No tag columns there; only comments, which are prose.
why.C: Table-level tags cannot name a column.
why.D: Records which mask applies, not why.

stem: During a repair, which tasks execute, and from where?

options.A: The failed tasks and their dependants, each from its own start; earlier successful tasks are not re-run.
options.B: Every task in the job, from the start.
options.C: Only the failed tasks, resuming from the failing statement.
options.D: The failed tasks and every task that ran before them.

explanation: Repair is selective and tasks are atomic units: a repaired task starts over, which is why it must be idempotent, and successful upstream commits are left standing.

why.B: That is a fresh run, not a repair.
why.C: Tasks have no resumable statements.
why.D: Upstream successes are precisely what repair skips.

stem: Which bundle command uploads files and creates or updates resources without running anything?

options.A: databricks bundle deploy
options.B: databricks bundle validate
options.C: databricks bundle run
options.D: databricks bundle sync --dry-run

explanation: validate checks configuration; deploy makes the workspace match it; run triggers a job or starts an app; a dry-run sync lists what would upload and changes nothing.

why.B: Creates nothing.
why.C: Executes a resource that deploy created.
why.D: Reports; does not upload.

stem: A point-in-time join uses valid_from <= d AND d <= valid_to. On changeover dates the fact count rises. Which single character fixes it?

options.A: Change the second <= to <, so a date matches exactly one version.
options.B: Change the first <= to <, so the first version is excluded.
options.C: Change AND to OR, so any version matches.
options.D: Change <= to = on both sides.

explanation: Validity windows are half-open: a version ends the instant the next begins. With inclusive bounds on both ends, an order on the changeover date matches the old and the new version.

why.B: Excludes the version that starts on the date, leaving those orders unmatched.
why.C: Matches every version of every customer, a far worse fan-out.
why.D: Matches only orders exactly on a boundary, dropping almost everything.

stem: Name the one operation that keeps partitioning preferable to liquid clustering for a table that overwrites whole date slices nightly.

options.A: REPLACE WHERE on the partition column; the old slice's files are dropped by metadata alone and only the new slice is written, where a clustered table must read and rewrite to do the same.
options.B: OPTIMIZE, which is only incremental on partitioned tables.
options.C: VACUUM, which cannot run on clustered tables.
options.D: MERGE, which requires partition pruning.

explanation: Clustering wins on almost everything except cheap slice replacement. When the workload is "drop this month and write it again" and the slices are large, partitioning is still the honest choice.

why.B: The opposite; OPTIMIZE is incremental on clustered tables.
why.C: VACUUM runs on any Delta table.
why.D: MERGE works on clustered tables and benefits from file skipping.
